summaries.example: Imagine a school day. You can say, “The bell rang earlier,” “Lunch will happen later,” or “After the bell, the class will stay quiet until the teacher arrives.” Temporal logic gives careful rules for statements like these.
summaries.summary: Temporal logic is the study of formal ways to represent time and reason about things that happen at different times. It grew partly from old philosophical questions, including whether a statement about a possible future event is already true or false. Modern temporal logic uses special symbols for ideas such as “sometime in the past,” “sometime in the future,” and “always in the future.” A model of time is a carefully chosen picture of how moments or periods are arranged. In an instant-based model, time is made from points. In an interval-based model, it is made from stretches. Time might be a straight line, a branching tree, or another structure. These choices affect what statements mean. Temporal logic is also used in computer science to describe what programs should do and to check that systems remain safe.
key_ideas: Temporal logic turns ideas about earlier, now, and later into precise rules.
Some models treat single moments as basic; others treat stretches of time as basic.
The future can be pictured as one line or as branches showing different possibilities.
Temporal logic is useful for talking about language, planning, artificial intelligence, and computer systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Temporal logic helps people make vague time statements more exact. It can help explain sentences in ordinary language, organize events in artificial intelligence, and test computer systems. For example, a designer can describe that every message should eventually receive a reply or that two traffic lights must never be green at the same time. The subject also shows that the way we picture time—moments, intervals, one future, or many possible futures—can change what we can say and prove.

important_terms.definition: A formal way to describe and reason about when things happen, such as in the past, present, or future.
A single location or point in time, such as 9:00 a.m.
A stretch of time with a beginning and an end, such as a class period.
A rule or symbol that says something happened before or will happen after something else.
A way of drawing time as a line, where each moment has one order compared with the others.

questions_to_think_about: Is a whole class period more useful to talk about than each second inside it?
Does the future have one fixed path, or could it have several possible paths?
What does “always” mean if there is a beginning or an end to time?
How could a computer check that a safety rule is never broken?

summaries.example: Suppose a program controls a railway signal. A temporal specification might say: whenever a train is detected, the signal remains red until the track becomes clear; every request for access is eventually answered; and two conflicting trains are never allowed onto the same track. A temporal logic does not merely describe one schedule. It describes patterns that must hold across the program’s possible runs.
summaries.summary:
Temporal logic broadly comprises formal methods for representing and reasoning about time. In its narrower and historically influential sense, it refers to the tense-logic tradition associated with Arthur Prior, which introduced temporal operators into propositional logic. Instead of treating propositions as entirely tenseless, tense logic evaluates them at a time and allows formulas to refer to earlier or later points. Operators can express that a formula was true at some earlier time, will be true at some later time, or has held throughout the past or will hold throughout the future. The semantics resembles modal logic: time instants take the role of possible worlds, and temporal precedence supplies the relevant accessibility relation.

A central modeling choice concerns temporal ontology. Instant-based models use points and a precedence ordering; interval-based models use periods and relations such as overlap, inclusion, and meeting. These approaches are technically related, but reduction between them does not settle whether formulas should be evaluated at instants or intervals. Temporal orderings can also be linear, discrete, dense, continuous, bounded, unbounded, or branching. A branching structure is often linear toward the past and divided toward the future, representing alternative histories. Peircean and Ockhamist approaches differ over how future claims are evaluated: one emphasizes all possible futures, while the other evaluates a claim relative to a selected history and adds quantification over histories.

Temporal logic has developed into many systems, including linear-time logic, branching-time logics, interval logics, metric and real-time logics, hybrid logics, and first-order temporal logics. These systems vary in expressive power and computational cost.
key_ideas: Temporal logic connects philosophical questions about tense, future contingency, modality, and change with formal semantics.
Prior’s tense logic extends propositional logic with operators for past, future, always-past, and always-future.
Temporal models differ by whether they use instants or intervals and by properties such as linearity, discreteness, density, beginnings, and endings.
In branching models, future claims may be evaluated along one history or across all possible histories, producing different logical systems.
Temporal logics can express requirements for computer programs, including safety, liveness, and fairness.
Technical expressiveness and computational tractability often pull in opposite directions: richer logics can describe more but may be harder or impossible to decide.
summaries.why_it_matters: Temporal logic supplies a bridge between abstract philosophy and practical formal reasoning. Philosophically, it clarifies disputes about tense, the open future, necessity, possibility, persistence, and the structure of time without assuming that one model settles those disputes. In linguistics, it helps analyze tense and aspect. In artificial intelligence, it represents events, actions, plans, and changing information. In computer science, it provides specifications for infinite or branching computations. important_terms.definition: A formal system for representing and reasoning about temporal information, including past, present, future, duration, and possible temporal orderings.
A primitive point in a temporal structure, ordered in relation to other points by precedence.
A period of time treated as a basic object, with relations such as before, overlap, inclusion, and meeting.
A symbol or expression that modifies a proposition by locating it in time, such as “sometime in the past” or “always in the future.”
A structure whose primitive temporal entities are instants and whose ordering is represented by a precedence relation.
A structure whose primitive entities are periods and whose relations describe how those periods are arranged.
A model in which time proceeds along one ordered path, rather than splitting into alternatives.
A model that is linear toward the past but allows several possible continuations toward the future.

questions_to_think_about: Can a statement about a future event have a definite truth value when several futures remain possible?
If intervals can be defined using endpoints and instants can be treated as point-intervals, why might the choice between them still matter semantically?
What is the difference between saying that something will happen on one selected history and saying that it will happen on every possible history?
Why might a more expressive temporal language make validity or satisfiability harder to determine?
Which properties of a system are best understood as safety requirements, and which as liveness requirements?

summaries.example: Think about a homework app. It should save your work whenever you press “save,” eventually show a confirmation, and never lose an already saved answer. A temporal logic can describe these rules: something good must happen later, something bad must never happen, and one action must continue until another event occurs. If the app can react in different ways, its future can be pictured as branches.
summaries.summary:
Temporal logic is a family of formal systems for reasoning about time. It studies how to represent statements about what was true, what is true now, what may become true, and what remains true. Its history reaches back to philosophical puzzles about change and future events. A major modern development came from Arthur Prior’s tense logic, which added operators to ordinary propositional logic. These operators can say that a statement held at some earlier point, will hold at some later point, or holds throughout the past or future.

To give a temporal logic meaning, we need a model of time. Instant-based models use points and a relation of precedence. They can be linear, like a line, or branching, like a tree whose past is shared but whose future has alternatives. They can also be discrete, with next moments, or dense, with another moment between any two moments. Interval-based models instead use periods and relations such as before, meeting, overlap, and containment. Although intervals can sometimes be built from endpoints and instants can be treated as zero-length intervals, the two approaches may still support different ways of interpreting language. Statements about an event lasting through a period may be more naturally handled by intervals.

Temporal logics have expanded in several directions. Linear-time systems describe one sequence of states; branching-time systems describe many possible computations. Operators such as “next,” “since,” and “until” make it possible to describe continuing processes. First-order temporal logics add objects, properties, and quantifiers, raising questions about which objects exist at which times. Hybrid and metric systems add references to particular times or exact durations. These choices influence both what can be expressed and how-
key_ideas: People have reasoned about time and future events since ancient philosophy, but modern temporal logic makes those questions formal.
Instant-based and interval-based models highlight different aspects of time: points and order versus periods and relations among periods.
Prior’s tense logic uses operators for past and future, while later systems add ideas such as next, until, and since.
A branching future creates a difference between what happens on one possible path and what happens on every possible path.
Temporal logic is used to describe natural-language tense, computer programs, plans, and intelligent systems.
Adding expressive features can make a logic more useful, but it can also make its decision problems difficult or undecidable.
summaries.why_it_matters: Temporal logic gives people a disciplined way to discuss change, persistence, possibility, and order. It helps linguists study tense and aspect, helps artificial-intelligence systems represent events and plans, and helps computer scientists specify and verify programs. For instance, a formal rule can require that every alert eventually receives a response while forbidding an unsafe state at every stage. The subject also teaches an important lesson about modeling: different assumptions about time can lead to different answers, so a model’s structure must be made explicit.

important_terms.definition: A precise language for describing how facts change or remain true over time.
One point in time. A model may order these points by which comes earlier or later.
A span of time, such as a meeting or a storm, considered as one object for reasoning.
An expression that changes the time meaning of a statement, such as “sometimes before,” “eventually,” or “always after.”
A time model in which moments form one ordered path.
A time model in which the past is shared but the future can split into alternative paths.
A property saying that a required good state will eventually be reached.
A property saying that an unwanted state never occurs.

questions_to_think_about: Would “the light was on during the whole evening” be better represented by an interval or by many separate instants?
How does a branching model represent an open future differently from a single timeline?
Why might “the request will eventually be answered” be a liveness rule, while “two users are never given the same private file” is a safety rule?
Can two models describe the same events but disagree about what counts as the basic part of time?
When should a formal system favor greater expressive power over easier computation?
